name: Audio Buffer London
description:
Audio Buffer London  is our monthly meet-up for audio developers and creative technologists—bridging the gap between academic theory and the gritty reality of releasing professional audio tools.
Led by Dr. Sinan Bokesoy, Audio Buffer is aimed at anyone developing software-hardware based music tools, be they students,  composers, academics, and other creative technologists. In a world of online isolation, we provide a physical environment to network, and stress-test ideas.
Audio Buffer 06 will be kindly hosted by Goldsmiths, University of London, during their annual Manifold Art event and exhibition.
"Old, But Not Obsolete" Zero-Inference Generative Systems
Session #06 of Audio Buffer London shifts focus to the foundational algorithms of computational creativity.
In the current era of AI, the conversation is dominated by massive, pre-trained transformer models. Yet, for live generative music, these modern monoliths face a critical flaw: latency. Gradient descent over billions of parameters cannot happen in 5ms.
This brings us to tonight's thesis:  Old, but not obsolete.  The algorithms that truly drive live, interactive generative performance are rooted in the mid-to-late 20th century—Markov chains, Cellular Automata, Stochastic distributions, and Evolutionary computing. These architectures do not rely on a frozen corpus or massive server farms. They are live, rule-based, on-the-fly processes with near-zero inference time. Because learning and generation happen simultaneously, they are instruments you  inhabit  rather than oracles you query.
Session #06 will examine four distinct applications built on these classic concepts, proving that foundational models still hold the key to real-time generative sonic art.
Registered attendees will receive a free license of Cosmosf M31.
Presenters
Prof. Matthew Yee-King,  "Clockwork" (Markov Chains) & "EvoSynth" (Genetic Algorithms)
Matthew presents two distinct systems spanning discrete logic and evolutionary computing. First, he introduces Clockwork, a custom Markov improviser that relies on explicit, real-time histograms built directly from the performer's input, implementing turn-taking as a physical quantity that charges and drains against a real clock.
He will also present EvoSynth, a system building upon concepts from his pioneering 2000 project  AudioServe . EvoSynth uses interactive genetic algorithms to search the space of all possible configurations for FM/AM synthesizer circuits. By cross-breeding small local "islands" of genomes, the system allows users to seamlessly mutate and discover novel waveforms on the fly.
Dr. Sinan Bökesoy  "Cosmosf M31" — Stochastic Distributions
Sinan presents his stochastic multi-scale MIDI event generator, Cosmosf M31. Rooted in the Xenakis lineage of aleatoric processes, M31 distributes discrete note events across varying time scales (macro, meso, micro) using a deep palette of stochastic functions. Instead of a pre-trained model guessing the next note, the performer continuously transforms a multi-dimensional parameter space in real time, navigating smoothly between rigidly ordered sequences and complex, disordered states.
Michael Wallis  "Cela" — Cellular Automata & Expressive Interfaces
Joining us from QMUL, Michael presents Cela, a MIDI controller designed to bridge the gap between musical skill and instrument playing. At its core is an 8x8 grid of toggles driven by the principles of Conway's Game of Life to autonomously generate evolving melodies and chords. Unlike models relying on vast data histories, Cela's memory is simply the current grid state. Michael will demonstrate how these hyper-local interactions create complex global sequences, while giving the performer deep expressive control through tactile BPM and ADSR parameters, alongside a physical light sensor that dynamically modulates the generated sound qualities.

name: Tour of Kirkaldy's  Testing Works including machine run
description:
Join us to tour David Kirkaldy's world-famous Testing & Experimenting Works and to see the Universal Testing Machine in action.

David Kirkaldy's Testing & Experimenting Works at 99 Southwark Street set the first international standards in materials testing; a science that has wide-reaching effects on everyday life today.

Today, this unique Victorian workshop keeps alive our direct link with Kirkaldy's innovation, at the heart of this bustling commercial district of London. Kirkaldy's Testing Works preserves Kirkaldy's unique Universal Testing Machine - the huge hydraulic powered machine he designed and had built in Leeds - in full working order in the premises he built to house it.

As well as presenting the story of the family who ran the business for almost 100 years and of the wider development of materials testing, the workshop and the Universal Testing Machine provide a unique crucible for new experimentation and collaboration - which can inspire future generations of scientists and artists alike to continue enquiring into the properties of the materials on which we build our lives.

Your tour around the Works will take about 2-hours 30-minutes including an introductory video, demonstrations of some of the smaller machines in our collection and will feature as its highlight a demonstration of the Universal Testing Machine.

At this time, we are not offering Concessions tickets or refunds due to problems with our financial security caused by the lockdown. We hope that you understand our position as a small museum fully reliant on ticket sales.

We're also now opening on some weekday evenings for shorter tours of the Museum. More info here.

Even in these strange times, we hope you'll join us in celebrating the vision of a forgotten hero of engineering science.

name: Can We Learn to Be Happier? What Science Says
description:
Can happiness be learned? Explore what positive psychology reveals about attention and the small habits that may help us thrive

Most of us imagine happiness will come after the next achievement, when life becomes less stressful, or when our circumstances finally improve.
But what if psychology tells a different story?
In this interactive Mind Circles Talk, Julia Coggins explores what positive psychology research can teach us about happiness, wellbeing and what it means to flourish.
Why does the mind seem so quick to notice problems, threats and what is going wrong? What actually influences our longer-term wellbeing? And can the way we direct our attention and shape our everyday habits make a meaningful difference?
Moving beyond the idea of simply “thinking positively”, Julia will explore the psychology behind happiness and how small, intentional changes in attention and behaviour may influence the way we experience everyday life.
Through research, reflection and interactive exercises, you’ll have the opportunity to put these ideas into practice and explore what may support your own wellbeing.
You’ll leave with:
A clearer understanding of the psychology of happiness, wellbeing and flourishing.
Insight into why the mind is naturally drawn to problems, threats and what is missing.
Practical ways to direct your attention towards what matters and what is working.
A simple, evidence-informed happiness habit to experiment with over the following week.
Ideas for making positive changes specific, realistic and sustainable in everyday life.
About Julia Coggins
Julia Coggins has more than 25 years’ experience in HR and employee relations, alongside over a decade designing and leading mental health and wellbeing initiatives.
As a Non-Clinical Mental Health & Wellbeing Lead, Julia worked in partnership with the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust (SLaM) Recovery College and the Maudsley Charity, supporting the development and delivery of practical approaches to mental wellbeing, resilience and positive behaviour change.
She has also designed and delivered successful workplace wellbeing programmes, workshops and initiatives focused on helping people think, work and feel better.
Today, Julia is a Positive Mindset and Wellbeing Coach, Barefoot-trained coach and NLP Practitioner, with a particular interest in positive psychology, happiness habits, mindset, resilience and behaviour change.
Through her transformational coaching, workplace programmes, talks and retreats, Julia combines her extensive professional experience with insights from positive psychology to help people turn understanding into action. Her approach focuses on small, sustainable changes that build confidence, strengthen resilience and help people lead happier, more fulfilling lives.

name: The History of Witchcraft & Women: Magic, rituals and the patriarchy
description:
Uncover the fascinating history of witchcraft and how patriarchal ideas shaped the image of a witch. Followed by Q&A.

The image of a female witch, with broom and black cat serving the devil, is ingrained in pop culture. But where did this stereotype come from? The concept of witchcraft emerged slowly over the course of several centuries as a result of theological, intellectual, and cultural changes in ideas about demons and heresy.
Magical practices were varied - including love magic, healing, and various forms of prognostication. And it certainly wasn’t always associated with women. In fact, more ‘sinister’ magic like necromancy - which relied heavily on the power of demons - was mostly done by men. This type of magic involved a lot of education that simply wasn’t accessible to women at the time. So how come this image of evil women practising magic - witches - came about?
This talk will use feminist approaches to the past to explore medieval changes in ideas about magic, gender, and heresy in order to better understand the emergence of witchcraft at the end of the middle ages. We will also look at witchcraft in relation to female sexuality and fears about women’s access to ritual power throughout history.
Doors open at 7pm, talk starts at 7.30pm - come down early to grab a good seat!
Follow us on IG @seedtalks
Dr Jennifer Farrell is a lecturer in medieval history at the University of Exeter. With interests in both gender and the medieval supernatural, her research and teaching focuses on cultural developments and their relationship to socio-political changes in Western Europe during the high and late middle ages (c. 1000- c. 1500). She has published on subjects including medieval prophecy; fairies in medieval history and romance; the relationship between literary representations of fairies, the supernatural, and gender; and is currently working on a book focused on Geoffrey of Monmouth and the origins of the Arthurian legends. Her teaching has included undergraduate and postgraduate courses looking at medieval gender and sexuality, universities and learning in the middle ages, magic in the middle ages, sexualities across time and space, and the legends of King Arthur.

## Details

Welcome to the DevSecOps London Gathering October Event on Wednesday 28 October! We bring you another night of great speakers, as well as the usual conversations, pizza and beer!

📍 Hosted at Autogen AI, 123 Pentonville Road, London, N1 9LG
📅 Wednesday, 28 October 2026
🕕 6:00–8:00 PM

## Talk Abstracts:

Talk 1 - Intent Graphs by Daramola Benjamin
An AI agent executing a task is filling in fields the user never specified. Book a flight to Dubai on Emirates, window seat, and cabin class, baggage, and refundability are all left open by default, not by choice. Sometimes the agent fills that gap with excess authority, a security failure. Sometimes it fills it with a wrong default, a correction failure. Both come from the same missing distinction.
This talk shows, from primary sources, where current standards stop. Web Bot Auth proves which agent sent a request but explicitly excludes the end user from its scope. RFC 8693 token exchange records a delegation chain but has no mechanism for capturing consent. Neither has an object for what a task actually was, which is a schema gap, not a cryptography gap.
The Intent Graph closes it: a shared schema where every task field is tagged declared or open dependency between fields is explicit, and revoking a permission or correcting a wrong outcome are the same graph operation at different points in time. The correction mechanism, causal scoping compensation, and an append only log, is walked through a flight booking where a wrong cabin class gets refunded and rebooked without touching the seat, the dates, or anything else that was already right.

The talk closes on the harder case: a structural material substitution and a surgical tool approaching an exclusion zone, where correction arrives too late to matter. One rule, the correction window of a field against the system's detection and response latency, decides whether the right response is fail open and correct after, or fail closed and verify before.
Speaker Bio:
Daramola Benjamin is an applied economist and engineer, and Head of Engineering at Levered. His current work is the Intent Graph, a schema and system architecture for identity, delegation, and correction in AI agent systems, closing the gap between what today's standards secure and what autonomous agents actually need. This work has produced a full system architecture, a research paper, a published technical analysis of agentic identity and permissioning, and a competitive review of the space. He has spoken on the Intent Graph at Practically AI, Manchester. Daramola designs systems and builds product end to end, with a background spanning fintech, commerce, and SaaS that shaped how he approaches identity and delegation as a systems problem with real consequences when it goes wrong.

The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) makes Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) a requirement for products in scope. Many teams are still tackling generation, but that is only the beginning. Real products contain multiple components, each with its own SBOM. Understanding what shipped means linking those SBOMs to specific releases and keeping that history useful for years.
Viktor Petersson co-led the CISA working group on SBOM generation. This talk starts with SBOM 101 and introduces sbomify-action, an open source, opinionated implementation of the blueprint developed by that group for generating high-quality SBOMs in CI/CD.
We then explore what happens after generation: retaining SBOMs, tracking components across releases, and putting the CRA’s ongoing vulnerability-handling requirements into practice. name: The Model is the Message - a talk on ML and AI: inference, ethics and the arts
description:
A free 1-hour talk by Marcel Top and Tessa Edwards on creativity and exploration in Machine Learning and AI as both the instrument and subject of societal critique and reflective self-evaluation. From deepfakes and facial recognition to digital privacy, surveillance and ethics around AI and creativity.

### About the Artists

[Marcel Top](https://www.instagram.com/marceltoptop/?hl=en "https://www.instagram.com/marceltoptop/?hl=en") is a visual artist working between Belgium and London. Top researches the topics of mass surveillance, privacy, data collection. In his practice, he layers a traditional approach to documentary research with a more experimental use of new technologies (such as facial recognition, movement analysis, and deepfakes). The artist uses these technologies to visualise and examine scenarios in which people can protect themselves and their rights by gaining knowledge and reclaiming control of surveillance tools.

Top’s work has been exhibited internationally, including FOMU Antwerp, Fotofestiwal Łódź, Athens Photo Festival, Circulation(s) and PhEST. He received the Encontros da Imagem Discovery Award for *Reversed Surveillance* (2024), the Prix Médiatine (2024), Folio #3 from the Institut pour la photographie (2023), and a PhMuseum Grant exhibition award (2022). His work is held in the collections of the University of the Arts London and the Institut pour la photographie in Lille.

[Tessa Edwards](https://www.instagram.com/babylon_kingkong?stkn=MTF1N2swdnZ4YTFxeg== "https://www.instagram.com/babylon_kingkong?stkn=MTF1N2swdnZ4YTFxeg==") is a creative technologist who moved from fashion into filmmaking and spatial computing before turning to machine learning. She treats ML as a material — working with its latent spaces, flaws, and logic as the medium itself. Her recent work spans deepfake analysis, psychoacoustics, and the use of steganography and hidden signals to explore perception, concealment, and the ways intelligent systems operate in dimensions beyond human reach. As an advocate for privacy and AI safety, Tessa’s work explores the ambiguities of ethical technology systems.

Curated by HQI.
Hosted by The Studio at White City Place.
